title: Between the Mongols and the Gunpowder Empires
subtitle: 1335–1517 · After the Ilkhans: Timur and the Timurids, Turkmen Confederations, the Mamluk Sultanate, the Rising Ottomans and the Safavid Order

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Jalayirids, Muzaffarids and Timur, the Timurid princes, the Turkmen confederations, the Mamluk sultans, the Ottomans and Shaykh Safi's heirs

entries.label: The end of Abu Said and the successor states
entries.hint: When Abu Said, the last effective Ilkhan, died in November 1335 without an heir, his state broke into the Jalayirids in Baghdad and Tabriz, the Chobanids in Azerbaijan, the Muzaffarids in Fars and Kirman, the Injuids in Shiraz, the Sarbadars in Khurasan and the Kartids at Herat, among generals and descendants of Genghis Khan's line; the Mongol legitimacy was held by puppet khans for some years.
entries.note: Hamdallah Mustawfi, Zafarnama; Jean Aubin; Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017); John Woods, The Aqquyunlu (1976).

entries.label: The Muzaffarids of Shiraz
entries.hint: The Muzaffarid dynasty, founded by Mubariz al-Din Muhammad, who took Yazd, Kirman and Shiraz, blinded his son Shah Shuja' (1358–1384) and was blinded in turn by him, was the patron of Hafez and Khwaju; its princes fought each other until Timur took Shiraz in 1387 and had the survivors killed in 1393, and the court of Shiraz is the setting of Hafez's ghazals.
entries.note: Mu'in al-Din Natanzi, Muntakhab al-tavarikh; Hafez, Divan; Jackson 2017; John Limbert, Shiraz in the Age of Hafez (2004).

entries.label: The Jalayirids of Baghdad and Tabriz
entries.hint: The Jalayirids, of a Mongol tribe, held Iraq and Azerbaijan after 1336 under Hasan Buzurg, Shaykh Uways and Sultan Ahmad (1382–1410), a patron of Persian poetry, music and painting who also wrote verse, and lost Baghdad to Timur in 1393 and 1401, to the Qara Qoyunlu in 1410; the Jalayirid atelier of Baghdad and Tabriz, with Khwaju Kermani's manuscripts, was the origin of the later Persian miniature.
entries.note: Jackson 2017; Wheeler Thackston, A Century of Princes (1989); Oleg Grabar and Sheila Blair, Epic Images and Contemporary History (1980).

entries.label: Timur
entries.hint: Timur, a Barlas Turk of Transoxiana, who rose from a band of followers to become the lord of Samarkand in 1370, conquered Khwarazm, Khurasan, Iran, Iraq, Georgia, Syria, India (Delhi 1398) and Anatolia (Ankara 1402), killed or enslaved populations at Isfahan, Baghdad and Delhi, built up Samarkand with the craftsmen of the conquered cities and died at Otrar on the way to China in February 1405.
entries.note: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah, Tamerlane; Beatrice Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989); Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane.

entries.label: Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg
entries.hint: Timur's youngest son Shah Rukh, who won the succession struggle by 1409 and ruled from Herat until 1447, restored the empire's stability and orthodox Sunni order, rebuilt Herat and was the patron of the arts and histories; his son Ulugh Beg governed Samarkand and the Transoxiana lands from 1409, established the observatory and the madrasas, and was killed in 1449 by order of his son Abd al-Latif after two years as supreme ruler.
entries.note: Hafiz-i Abru, Zubdat al-tavarikh; Abd al-Razzaq Samarqandi, Matla' al-sa'dayn; Manz, Power, Politics and Religion in Timurid Iran (2007).

entries.label: Husayn Bayqara
entries.hint: Sultan Husayn Bayqara, a great-great-grandson of Timur who took Herat in 1469 and ruled until 1506, kept a court that was the last great cultural centre of the Timurid world, with the poets Jami and Mir Ali Shir Navai, the painter Bihzad, the historian Khvandamir and the Naqshbandi shaykhs, even as his sons fought each other and the Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan took the city in 1507.
entries.note: Khvandamir, Habib al-siyar; Babur, Baburnama; Maria Subtelny, Timurids in Transition (2007).

entries.label: The Qara Qoyunlu and Jahan Shah
entries.hint: The Black Sheep Turkmen, of Lake Van and Mosul, who defeated the Jalayirids, were driven out by Timur and returned under Qara Yusuf after 1405, held Azerbaijan, Iraq and western Iran under Jahan Shah (1438–1467), who built the Blue Mosque of Tabriz and took Herat in 1458, before being killed by the Aq Qoyunlu in 1467.
entries.note: Woods 1976; Sharaf al-Din Yazdi; Thackston 1989; Minorsky, ‘Jihan-shah Qara-qoyunlu’ (1954).

entries.label: Uzun Hasan and the Aq Qoyunlu
entries.hint: Uzun Hasan, who took the leadership of the White Sheep confederation of the Diyarbakır region in 1453, destroyed the Qara Qoyunlu in 1467 and the Timurid Abu Said at Karabagh in 1468, took Tabriz and western Iran, allied with Venice, married a Trebizond princess, and was beaten by Mehmed II at Otlukbeli in 1473; his successors Yaqub and Rustam were pulled down by the Safavids from 1501.
entries.note: Woods 1976; Tihrani, Kitab-i Diyarbakriyya; Josafa Barbaro, Travels to Tana and Persia; Ottoman chronicles.

entries.label: Barquq to Qaytbay
entries.hint: The Circassian Burji Mamluk sultans, from Barquq in 1382 to Qaytbay (1468–1496), ruled Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz, with the revenue of iqtas, the Red Sea trade and the pilgrimage, surviving Timur's attack on Aleppo and Damascus in 1400–1401, the Aq Qoyunlu and Ottomans on the Taurus frontier, and the shortages of the plague years; Qaytbay's reign had the last stable years before the Ottoman war.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, Suluk; Ibn Taghribirdi, al-Nujum al-zahira; Carl Petry, Twilight of Majesty (1993); Robert Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986).

entries.label: Shaykh Safi's order and Ismail
entries.hint: The Safavid Sufi order, founded by Shaykh Safi al-Din of Ardabil (d. 1334), a Sunni of the Shafi'i rite, became under his descendants Junayd (d. 1460), Haydar (d. 1488) and Ismail a militant Shia movement with Turkmen disciples, called Qizilbash after the red hats of its twelve-pointed headdress; Ismail, aged fourteen, took Tabriz in 1501 and was crowned Shah.
entries.note: Ibn Bazzaz, Safvat al-safa; Michel Mazzaoui, The Origins of the Safawids (1972); Roger Savory, Iran under the Safavids (1980).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Black Death years, Timur's campaigns, Ankara, Otlukbeli, the Mamluk–Ottoman war and Chaldiran

entries.label: The wars of the successor states
entries.hint: Chobanid and Jalayirid armies fought in Azerbaijan and Iraq, the Injuid and Muzaffarid rulers of Shiraz, the Kartids and the Sarbadars (a Shiite-leaning popular movement of Sabzavar), and the Black Death in 1347–1349 and the first Golden Horde invasion of Tabriz in 1357 deepened the disorder that Timur later used.
entries.note: Jackson 2017; Mustawfi; Jean Aubin, ‘Réseau pastoral et réseau caravanier’ (1971).

entries.label: Timur's three- and five-year campaigns
entries.hint: In the Three-Year Campaign of 1386–1388 Timur took Isfahan, where the revolt of the inhabitants against his tax collectors was followed by the massacre of some 70,000, and Shiraz, and in the Five-Year Campaign of 1392–1396 he took Mazandaran, Baghdad, Georgia and Armenia and defeated Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde on the Terek in 1395, having his armies build towers of skulls at the cities that resisted.
entries.note: Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah; Manz 1989; Clavijo.

entries.label: Delhi, Aleppo and Damascus
entries.hint: Timur took Delhi in December 1398, sacking it for five days, and in 1400–1401 defeated the Mamluk army at Aleppo, took Damascus, where he met the historian Ibn Khaldun, and sacked it, taking its craftsmen to Samarkand, and in 1401 destroyed Baghdad with the killing of tens of thousands; the Mamluk sultan Faraj was left to recover.
entries.note: Zafarnama; Ibn Khaldun, Autobiography; Ibn Arabshah; Walter Fischel, Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane (1952).

entries.label: The battle of Ankara
entries.hint: Bayezid I, who had taken the Anatolian emirates and refused to return their lands, met Timur's army of perhaps 140,000 at Çubuk near Ankara on 20 July 1402, and, with his Anatolian emirs' troops going over to their old masters and his Serbs the last to fight, was defeated and captured; Timur restored the emirates and Bayezid died in captivity, so that the Ottoman state broke up for a decade.
entries.note: Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah; Dukas; Clavijo; Dimitris Kastritsis, The Sons of Bayezid (2007).

entries.label: Otlukbeli
entries.hint: Mehmed II, with an army of Ottoman cavalry and a large body of Janissaries and cannon, met Uzun Hasan at Otlukbeli in the upper Euphrates, defeated him decisively with firearms, which the Turkmen horsemen lacked, and opened Anatolia to the Ottomans, while the Aq Qoyunlu state was weakened.
entries.note: Neşri; Woods 1976; Barbaro; Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002).

entries.label: The Mamluk–Ottoman war over Cilicia
entries.hint: Over the vassal state of Dulkadir and the Cilician marches the Mamluks of Qaytbay fought Bayezid II's armies for six years in a war that ended with a stalemate and a peace in 1491, in which the Mamluks, with their horsemen's reluctance to use handguns, held their frontier; it was the first clash that showed the two systems.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i' al-zuhur; Petry 1993; Imber 2002.

entries.label: Chaldiran
entries.hint: Selim I met Shah Ismail's Qizilbash cavalry at Chaldiran, where the Ottoman artillery and Janissary muskets broke the charge, and took Tabriz for a few days; the battle set the Ottoman–Safavid frontier and showed that firearms had made the nomad cavalry state obsolete, and Ismail, who had thought himself invincible, never again led his army.
entries.note: Hasan-i Rumlu, Ahsan al-tavarikh; Idris Bitlisi; Savory 1980; Imber 2002.

entries.label: The fall of the Mamluks
entries.hint: Selim defeated the Mamluk army of Qansuh al-Ghawri at Marj Dabiq on 24 August 1516, where Qansuh was killed, and on 22 January 1517 at Raydaniyya, outside Cairo, Tumanbay's cavalry, who had refused to use guns, failed against the Ottoman artillery; the Ottomans entered Cairo, hanged Tumanbay and ended the sultanate.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas vol. 5; Petry, Protectors or Praetorians? (1994); Imber 2002.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Turkmen tribal state, Timur's nomad-sedentary compromise, the Mamluk iqta and the rise of the sultanate of Rum's heirs

entries.label: The Mamluk iqta and the rawk
entries.hint: The Mamluk state paid its soldiers by iqta, assignments of village revenue surveyed in the cadastral survey of 1315, which Sultan Barquq and his successors adapted and, after the plague, the army's shares were revised in rawks, and the sultan's tax farm (damans) and monopolies on spices and sugar supported the court; the effects of the plague on the iqta revenue and the Bedouin raids on the villages led to a long fiscal crisis.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, Khitat; Ayalon, Studies on the Mamluks of Egypt (1977); Petry 1993.

entries.label: Timur's imperial system
entries.hint: Timur ruled in the name of a Chinggisid puppet khan, under the Mongol law of Genghis Khan (yasa) with a tribal nobility of emirs from the Barlas, Jalayir and other clans and a Persian bureaucracy of taxation; he used terror, deportations of craftsmen and sacred patronage (shrines at Turkestan, Samarkand and Mashhad) to unite them.
entries.note: Manz 1989; Zafarnama; Beatrice Manz, ‘Tamerlane and the Symbolism of Sovereignty’, Iranian Studies 21 (1988).

entries.label: The Turkmen confederations
entries.hint: The Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu states were confederations of pastoral clans under the paramount house, with an army of tribal cavalry, their lands held by emirs as tribal grants and the settled provinces under Persian officials; the system lacked a stable succession rule, as the many struggles between princes after Jahan Shah and Uzun Hasan show.
entries.note: Woods 1976; John Woods, ‘The Rise of Timurid Historiography’, Journal of Near Eastern Studies 46 (1987); Jackson 2017.

entries.label: Hasan Beg's law and the Ottoman kanun
entries.hint: Uzun Hasan's kanunname of about 1470, whose text on taxes and land was handed down in later collections as the Qanun-i Uzun Hasan, abolished some arbitrary taxes and codified tribal and civil law in the Aq Qoyunlu state; it was a model for Safavid and Ottoman legislation, as were the Ottoman codes of Mehmed II.
entries.note: Minorsky, ‘A Civil and Military Review in Fars in 881/1476’ (1939); Woods 1976.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Sufi orders, Naqshbandis and Hurufis, Shiism and the Safavid rise, and the Mamluk ulema

entries.label: The rise of Shiism and the Safavid claim
entries.hint: Shiite sentiment, often in a mystical form, spread with the Mongol collapse among Turkmen and urban groups, among them the Sarbadars, the Mar'ashi sayyids of Mazandaran and the Musha'sha' of Khuzestan; Junayd, Haydar and Ismail built a Sufi Shiite militant order with a claim of descent from the Seventh Imam, and with the poems of Khata'i, Ismail's own pen-name, in Turkish proclaimed him divine.
entries.note: Savory 1980; Mazzaoui 1972; Shah Ismail, Divan (Khata'i); Kathryn Babayan, Mystics, Monarchs, and Messiahs (2002).

entries.label: The Mamluk ulema and the shrines
entries.hint: The Mamluk sultans were the patrons of a large body of Sunni jurists, preachers and Sufis in Cairo and Damascus, among them al-Suyuti (d. 1505), al-Maqrizi (d. 1442), Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 1449) and al-Sakhawi, and of the shrines of the family of the Prophet; the sultans' Abbasid caliph, kept in Cairo from 1261, was a symbolic figure whose investiture they sought.
entries.note: Jonathan Berkey, The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo (1992); Petry 1993.

entries.label: The Naqshbandis and Khwaja Ahrar
entries.hint: The Naqshbandi order, founded by Baha al-Din Naqshband (d. 1389) at Bukhara, which stressed silent dhikr, the sharia and engagement in the world, became under Khwaja Ahrar (1404–1490) a political force in Samarkand and Herat, with landholdings and advice to the Timurid rulers; Jami was a member, and the order spread to India and the Ottomans.
entries.note: Jurgen Paul, Die politische und soziale Bedeutung der Naqšbandiyya in Mittelasien (1991); Hamid Algar; Subtelny 2007.

entries.label: The Hurufis
entries.hint: Fadl Allah Astarabadi, who taught that the letters of the alphabet and the face of man held the divine secret and proclaimed himself a manifestation of God in Tabriz, was executed at Alinja near Nakhchivan in 1394 on the orders of Timur's son Miran Shah; his followers spread in Anatolia and the Balkans, as in the poetry of Nesimi (executed in Aleppo in 1417) and the Bektashi order.
entries.note: Shahzad Bashir, Fazlallah Astarabadi and the Hurufis (2005); Fadlallah, Javidan-nama.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Hafez, Jami and Navai, Behzad and Bihzad's school, Samarkand and Herat, and the Mamluk buildings of Cairo

entries.label: Hafez of Shiraz
entries.hint: Shams al-Din Muhammad Hafez, a Qur'an reciter and teacher at the Muzaffarid court, whose ghazals of love, wine and the tavern, with their multiple meanings of mystical and worldly love, and praise of the rulers made him the great poet of Persian lyric, is said by tradition to have met Timur in Shiraz in 1387; his tomb in Shiraz is a place of pilgrimage and his Divan is used in divination.
entries.note: Hafez, Divan (ed. Qazvini-Ghani); Limbert 2004; Hafez (trans. Dick Davis, 2012).

entries.label: The Mamluk monuments of Cairo
entries.hint: The madrasa-mosque of Sultan Hasan (1356–1363), with its 36-metre portal and four iwans, the funerary complexes of Barquq (1384–1386) and Qaytbay (1472–1474) in the Northern Cemetery, with their stone domes carved in stars and arabesques, and the many domes of the Mamluk period make Cairo the city of the thousand minarets.
entries.note: Doris Behrens-Abouseif, Cairo of the Mamluks (2007); Irwin 1986.

entries.label: Samarkand: the Gur-e Amir, the Registan and the Bibi Khanum
entries.hint: Timur, with craftsmen taken from Damascus, Shiraz and Delhi, built the Bibi Khanum mosque (1399–1404), the Gur-e Amir mausoleum (1403–1404) with its fluted turquoise dome, and the Shah-i Zinda necropolis; Ulugh Beg added a madrasa on the Registan (1417–1420) and the observatory, in a style of large scale and tile mosaic that defined the image of the Timurid city.
entries.note: Lisa Golombek and Donald Wilber, The Timurid Architecture of Iran and Turan (1988); Clavijo; Lentz and Lowry 1989.

entries.label: Jami, Navai and Bihzad
entries.hint: Abd al-Rahman Jami (1414–1492), poet, Sufi and scholar, wrote the Haft awrang, the last great Persian classic; Mir Ali Shir Navai (1441–1501), minister of Husayn Bayqara, made Chagatai Turkish a literary language; Kamal al-Din Bihzad (c. 1450–1535) painted manuscripts for the court of Herat in a style of detail and naturalism that was taken to Tabriz, Bukhara and the Safavid ateliers.
entries.note: Jami, Haft awrang; Navai, Muhakamat al-lughatayn; Thomas Lentz and Glenn Lowry, Timur and the Princely Vision (1989); Subtelny 2007.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibn Khaldun, Ulugh Beg's observatory, al-Maqrizi and the Timurid historians

entries.label: Ibn Khaldun
entries.hint: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406), a Tunisian jurist who served rulers from Granada to Cairo, wrote in 1377 the Muqaddima, an introduction to the study of history that set out a theory of the cycle of dynasties through the asabiyya (group feeling) of nomads and urban civilisation and its decline, and in 1401 had a meeting with Timur outside Damascus, whom he described to the sultan; he died in Cairo.
entries.note: Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddima (trans. Franz Rosenthal, 1958); Autobiography; Fischel 1952; Robert Irwin, Ibn Khaldun (2018).

entries.label: Al-Maqrizi and the Mamluk historians
entries.hint: Taqi al-Din al-Maqrizi (1364–1442) wrote the Khitat, a topography of Cairo and Egypt with its history, the Suluk, a chronicle of the Mamluks, and a treatise on the famines of Egypt (Ighathat al-umma) that explained the crisis of 1403–1405 by bad government and coin debasement; Ibn Taghribirdi, al-Ayni and Ibn Hajar belong to the same school of Mamluk history.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, Khitat; Ighathat al-umma (trans. Allouche, 1994); Ibn Taghribirdi; Irwin 1986.

entries.label: The Timurid historians
entries.hint: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's Zafarnama (1425), Hafiz-i Abru's Zubdat al-tavarikh, Abd al-Razzaq's Matla' al-sa'dayn, Mirkhvand's Rawdat al-safa and his grandson Khvandamir's Habib al-siyar, written for Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara, the main court histories of the age, depict Timur as a lawful and world-conquering ruler with a divinely sanctioned destiny.
entries.note: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi; Hafiz-i Abru; Khvandamir; Woods 1987; Subtelny 2007.

entries.label: Ulugh Beg's observatory and the Zij-i Sultani
entries.hint: Ulugh Beg built, between 1424 and 1429, an observatory at Samarkand with a giant sextant of 40 metres' radius, cut into a hill, and with the astronomers Qadi Zada al-Rumi and Ali Qushji produced the Zij-i Sultani, a catalogue of 1,018 stars and a table of planetary positions (completed 1437) that was the most exact since Ptolemy; the observatory was destroyed after his death.
entries.note: Ulugh Beg, Zij-i Sultani; Sevim Tekeli; Edward Kennedy, ‘A Survey of Islamic Astronomical Tables’ (1956); Stephen Dale, The Muslim Empires (2010).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The Black Death, the trade routes and the Italian cities, the Mamluk spice monopoly and the Portuguese challenge

entries.label: The Black Death and its returns
entries.hint: The Black Death reached Alexandria in October 1347 and Cairo and Damascus in 1348, in which perhaps a third of the population died according to Ibn al-Wardi, al-Maqrizi and others, and returned in 1361, 1374, 1403 and often thereafter, so that the population and tax revenue of Egypt fell for a century; the rural land was abandoned and the Bedouin took over some.
entries.note: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977); al-Maqrizi, Suluk; Ibn al-Wardi, Risalat al-naba' 'an al-waba'; Stuart Borsch, The Black Death in Egypt and England (2005).

entries.label: The Mamluk spice monopoly and the Karimi merchants
entries.hint: The Mamluks, under Barsbay (1422–1438), made themselves sole buyers of pepper and fixed its price and that of other spices at Jeddah, taxing the Karimi merchants of Cairo, who had financed the trade between Aden, Cairo and Venice; Venetian and Genoese merchants bought at Alexandria and Damascus, and the system was a main source of revenue until the Portuguese Cape route after 1498.
entries.note: Eliyahu Ashtor, Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages (1983); S. D. Goitein, A Mediterranean Society; Petry 1993.

entries.label: The Timurid revival of the caravan routes
entries.hint: Under Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg the roads from China through Herat to Tabriz and the ports were reopened, with an embassy to the Ming court of Yongle (1419–1422) and caravanserais, bridges and a postal system; the Silk Road trade, which had been damaged by the Mongol disorder, revived until the end of the century.
entries.note: Hafiz-i Abru; Abd al-Razzaq; Manz 2007; Hansen, The Silk Road (2012).

entries.label: The Portuguese challenge and Hormuz
entries.hint: After Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut in 1498, the Portuguese undertook the blockade of the Red Sea and Gulf entrances, took Goa in 1510 and Hormuz in 1507 and, again in 1515; the Mamluk fleet sent by Qansuh al-Ghawri was defeated at Diu in 1509 and the revenue of the Cairo spice trade shrank in the last decades.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; João de Barros, Décadas; Petry 1993; Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia (1993).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The first cannon, the Samarkand observatory and the Mamluk resistance to firearms

entries.label: The Samarkand sextant and the Maragha tradition
entries.hint: Ulugh Beg's large instrument, the Fakhri sextant, a masonry arc of some 40 metres' radius set in a trench in the Kohak hill, found by the Russian archaeologist Vyatkin in 1908, was the largest of its kind and the main source of its stellar and planetary observations, standing in the tradition of the observatory of Maragha of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi.
entries.note: Vasily Vyatkin, excavations (1908); Zij-i Sultani; Kennedy 1956.

entries.label: The resistance to firearms and the Ottoman guns
entries.hint: The Mamluks used cannon for sieges and had a unit of handgun (barud) men from the 1460s, but their cavalry class, the royal mamluks, scorned firearms and the Ottomans with their Janissary musketeers and field cannon used these at Otlukbeli, Chaldiran and Raydaniyya to win, as the Mamluk and Safavid chroniclers noted, while the Safavid state later took the technology.
entries.note: David Ayalon, Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom (1956); Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005); Savory 1980.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Timur's embassies, the Ming treasure fleets, the Italian merchants and the Ottoman–Venetian wars

entries.label: Venice, Genoa and the Mamluk and Ottoman markets
entries.hint: Venice and Genoa, which in the fourteenth century held the trade of the Levant, took spices, silk and cotton in Alexandria, Beirut and Damascus, with consuls and funduqs under treaties with the Mamluks, and began in the fifteenth century to trade in Ottoman Bursa and Constantinople; after the papal ban on trade with Egypt and the crusade of 1365 the Venetian relations with the Mamluks and the Ottomans were conditioned by the Aegean war.
entries.note: Ashtor 1983; Halil İnalcık, ‘Bursa and the Commerce of the Levant’ (1960); Nicol, Byzantium and Venice (1988).

entries.label: The embassies to Timur and the Ming
entries.hint: Henry III of Castile sent Ruy González de Clavijo to Timur in 1403–1406, who described Samarkand; the Ming emperor Yongle and Shah Rukh exchanged embassies in 1407–1422, with Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash's journey to Beijing in 1419–1422 and the Chinese envoys to Herat, and Chinese sources show the Zheng He fleets reaching Hormuz and Jeddah in 1413–1433.
entries.note: Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane; Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash's diary (in Hafiz-i Abru); Louise Levathes, When China Ruled the Seas (1994).

entries.label: The Aq Qoyunlu and Venice
entries.hint: Venice sent embassies to Uzun Hasan in 1463–1478 under Caterino Zeno, Josafa Barbaro and Ambrogio Contarini to coordinate an eastern front against Mehmed II, with a supply of arms and a promise of Venetian guns; Uzun Hasan's defeat at Otlukbeli in 1473 and the promised firearms that were never delivered ended the alliance.
entries.note: Barbaro and Contarini, Travels to Tana and Persia (1873); Woods 1976; Setton, The Papacy and the Levant vol. 2 (1978).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The plague, the Little Ice Age and the Turkmen migration

entries.label: The fourteenth-century crisis and the Little Ice Age
entries.hint: The weather, with colder and wetter summers in the Alps and Europe and a series of poor floods of the Nile and droughts in Syria and Iran, may have been part of the change of climate that began in the early fourteenth century, along with the plague, to reduce the population; al-Maqrizi's accounts of the Nile and famines of 1403–1405 record the effects.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, Ighathat al-umma; Dols 1977; Bruce Campbell, The Great Transition (2016).

entries.label: The Turkmen migration and the settlement of Anatolia
entries.hint: The movement of Turkmen tribes from the Iranian plateau and Central Asia, enlarged by Timur's wars, continued to settle Anatolia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and northern Iraq and changed the character of the Aq Qoyunlu and Safavid movements, and the lands of the Byzantine and Armenian populations became Turkish; the deportations of Timur carried others to Transoxiana.
entries.note: Woods 1976; Cahen, Pre-Ottoman Turkey (1968); Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism (1971).

entries.label: The destruction of Baghdad and the cities of Timur
entries.hint: Timur's capture of Baghdad in 1401, with the killing of tens of thousands and the building of some 120 towers of skulls by the accounts of the chroniclers, and the earlier sack of Isfahan, with its reputed 70,000 killed, caused deep and long damage to the old cities of the plateau and Iraq, whose irrigation and urban life never recovered in many places.
entries.note: Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah; Manz 1989.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Gawhar Shad, the Timurid scholars, Ibn Battuta's Iran and the pilgrims

entries.label: Ibn Battuta in Iran and the Ilkhanate
entries.hint: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited the Ilkhanid lands in 1327 and the Mamluk Syria and Egypt in 1326 and 1348, described Shiraz, Isfahan, Baghdad, Tabriz and Basra on the eve of the Ilkhanate's collapse and saw plague in Damascus in 1348; his Rihla is a main source for the daily life of the cities and the pilgrimage.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (trans. H. A. R. Gibb, 1958–2000); Ross Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta (1986).

entries.label: Bibi Khanum and the women of Timur's family
entries.hint: The women of Timur's house, among them Saray Mulk Khanum, his chief wife and a descendant of Genghis Khan, who built the Bibi Khanum madrasa, and Tuman Agha and Tolun Agha, had their own households and endowments and travelled with the court, as Clavijo describes in the festival of 1404 in Samarkand.
entries.note: Clavijo; Manz 2007; Golombek and Wilber 1988.

entries.label: The deported craftsmen and the peasants of Timur
entries.hint: Timur deported craftsmen, architects, scholars and artists from the cities he conquered, among them Damascus, Shiraz, Tabriz, Aleppo, Delhi and Ankara, to Samarkand, whose population he increased with their families, and left the peasants of the conquered lands, under the heavy taxation of his officers, to starve; the later Mamluk chronicles record the massacres of Aleppo and Damascus.
entries.note: Ibn Arabshah; Zafarnama; Ibn Khaldun; Manz 1989.

entries.label: Gawhar Shad
entries.hint: Gawhar Shad (d. 1457), the wife of Shah Rukh and a Turkish noblewoman, built the great mosque at the shrine of Imam Reza in Mashhad (1405–1418), her own mosque and madrasa at Herat and a mosque in Herat that bears her name, and led the court's politics after the king's death in 1447 until her execution at 80 in 1457 by Abu Sa'id; she is the most important patron of her age.
entries.note: Hafiz-i Abru; Abd al-Razzaq; Golombek and Wilber 1988; Subtelny 2007.
